attribution.note: Zitron's own words on his blog, restating his earlier hypothesis in the first person.

semantics.note: The antecedent and the 'at the very least' fallback are both kept. 'I hypothesize' signals tentative confidence, so the drafter's 'likely' modality fits, and hedged forecasts are not scored.

contract.note: The antecedent and causal-chain criteria are reasonable. But a plain reading applies only to firm language, and this claim is hedged by 'I hypothesize', so the contract cannot score it. Whether the antecedent occurred is also unknown.

evidence.note: Cursor changed its own pricing because token use rose. This is a downstream price change, not a provider repricing to cover costs.
Anthropic list price for Opus 4.5. It gives no cost-coverage information, so it does not establish the antecedent.

reviews.rationale: 'I hypothesize' is a hedged, tentative prediction, so policy says it is not scored. Separately, the evidence does not show that the antecedent (OpenAI or Anthropic pricing to cover their costs) ever happened, and there is no deadline.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his blog post.

semantics.note: Firm factual claim about past spending, with the threshold and 'last year' window kept.

contract.note: Reading the window as the trailing twelve months and counting only realized spending is an ordinary reading. Company coverage and how much spending counts as generative AI remain open, as the contract notes.

evidence.note: One Microsoft quarter of combined cloud-and-AI capex. It is not an industry-wide trailing-year total and does not separate out generative AI.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only one company's capex for one quarter, with no generative-AI split. No aggregate for the twelve months to December 2024 is supplied, so the evidence can neither confirm nor reject the over-$200B figure.

attribution.note: Zitron's own summary statement in the post.

semantics.note: Combines the firm 'has peaked' with the hedged 'may have reached Peak AI'. Only the firm part is scorable, and the contract handles it that way.

contract.note: Reading 'peaked' as a capability plateau with weaker returns from data and compute, over 2024 up to publication, is ordinary. The hedged 'may have' part is not scored.

evidence.note: OpenAI reports o1 well ahead of GPT-4o on reasoning benchmarks in Sept 2024. This counts against a peak, but it is OpenAI's own disclosure, not an independent test.
Reuters, Nov 2024: reported delays and Sutskever's view that pretraining has plateaued. This supports diminishing returns from scaling up pretraining.

reviews.rationale: The part that holds: Reuters reporting supports diminishing returns from scaling up pretraining before the post. The part that fails: o1's reported benchmark gains, within the same period, cut against the broader claim that the technology had peaked. Those gains are company-reported only.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his blog post.

semantics.note: The checkable core is the categorical claim that the products cost more to serve than customers pay. 'Dead-end' and 'inessential' are value judgments and are left unscored.

contract.note: Reading 'cost to serve' as inference and hosting cost is the ordinary meaning and not stretched. Using 2024, the year of the surrounding financial discussion, is reasonable.

evidence.note: Epoch, citing The Information: OpenAI's 2024 revenue of $4B against $2.4B in inference and hosting costs, about a 40% gross margin. These are estimates from reporting, not audited figures.
FutureSearch says its own API-only margin estimates remain unverified. It mentions reported positive 2024 compute margins, but this item is not relied on.

reviews.rationale: The claim is categorical: products cost more to serve than anyone would pay. The reported figures give OpenAI's 2024 revenue as well above its inference and hosting costs, which is a counterexample. The figures are reported estimates. The claim about company-wide profitability is a separate matter and is not tested here.
